text: A primary exchange currency converts one resource into another, adding a layer that lets designers adjust the exchange rate over time.
Price a tier 1 item so it seems attainable at tier 1 and nearly free by tier 3, letting players feel their growing economic power.
when: Balancing prices across tiers
why: Shifting affordability across tiers makes progression feel like growing power

text: Price bulk consumables by tier so higher-tier food costs more per unit than lower-tier food.
when: Designing shop consumables across tiers
why: Tiered pricing matches the value of stronger consumables

text: Each manually purchased tier 1 building boosts all tier 1 production by 0.05 percent, keeping manual purchases valuable even with billions of free units.
when: Lower tiers are produced for free by higher tiers.
why: A per-purchase boost gives manual purchases lasting value.

text: Resources with two uses create decisions such as processing versus selling, or spending now versus saving for a later use.
when: Each resource has at least two uses
why: Competing uses force players to choose how to allocate scarce output

when: Setting prices and income for an idle RPG with four tiers
why: Matching prices to income keeps purchases meaningful at each tier

text: Set shop prices near thirty to sixty minutes of farming earnings, scaled to each item's tier.
when: Pricing shop items in an idle game
why: This keeps items attainable within a session while still requiring saving

text: Cooked food heals in combat by tier: tier 1 gives 3 HP, tier 2 gives 5 HP, tier 3 gives 10 HP, tier 4 gives 14 HP, tier 5 gives 20 HP.
when: Setting healing values for cooked food
why: Rising healing per tier rewards higher-level cooking

text: Gathering yield multiplier is 1.00 below mastery 25, up to +3% at mastery 25 to 49, up to +7% at mastery 50 to 98, and 1.10 at mastery 99.
when: Applying mastery yield bonus to gathering

text: An economy needs faucets (currency sources) and sinks (spending places), or currency accumulates until it becomes meaningless.
when: Designing an idle game economy
why: Currency without spending opportunities stops mattering to players

text: A resource economy has four kinds: primary resources are abundant and used broadly; secondary resources need processing; tertiary resources are rare and gate progression; currency is a universal exchange.
when: Designing the resource structure of a game
why: Each tier plays a different role in creating choices and pacing

text: Lower tiers can become irrelevant to buy because higher tiers already grow them for free.
when: Designing a derivative chain without tier interaction.
why: Automated production removes the need to purchase lower tiers.

text: Use each dungeon's unique reward in at least one crafting recipe or give it a meaningful stat bonus; otherwise it loses relevance after its first clear.
when: Designing dungeon reward items
why: Players have no further use for an unused reward once obtained

text: Give every resource at least two distinct uses, such as fuel, crafting input, or sale for currency; a single use leaves players no real choice.
when: Designing or reviewing resources in an economy
why: A single use gives players no real choice

text: Give every content tier at least one meaningful currency sink.
when: Designing currency sinks across tiers
why: Sinks in each tier keep currency meaningful as income grows

text: Use direct purchase for items that skip a crafting step, but price them high enough that crafting stays relevant.
when: Selling crafted-equivalent items in a shop
why: Cheap shortcuts make crafting pointless

text: Full offline earnings make active play feel pointless, so offline rewards should keep being present better than being absent.
when: Setting offline reward rate
why: Equal offline reward removes incentive to play actively

text: Prestige currency can be computed from max earnings, lifetime earnings, earnings since last reset, or upgrades bought since last reset.
When progression hits a wall, introduce a fresh decision instead of extending the waiting time.
when: Progress stalls at a wall in an idle game
why: A new choice changes the optimization problem, while longer waits only extend the stall

text: When designing allocation choices, ask what resource currently caps growth, and whether short-term output is worth a long-term cost.
when: Evaluating idle production choices

text: With lifetime or max-based prestige, doubling prestige currency requires earning several times the previous run, so players must keep progressing.
when: Designing lifetime or max-based prestige formulas.
why: Currency is tied to cumulative past performance.

text: With since-reset prestige, resetting at the same point repeatedly yields the same currency, so replaying the same point stays rewarding.
when: Designing since-reset prestige formulas.
why: Currency is independent of previous runs.

text: Treating a simulation's output as an accurate prediction of player behavior is a mistake; use it as a rough guide.
when: Interpreting balance simulation results.
why: Players deviate from modeled reset behavior.

text: Under a flat since-reset curve, ideal strategy may involve little progress beyond a certain point, so such systems need very different balancing.
when: Using flat since-reset prestige curves.
why: Returns flatten, making further progress unrewarding.

text: A stall with no layer, event, or reset beyond it turns into an exit instead of a difficulty spike.
when: A stall has no reset, layer or event beyond it
why: Players see no future payoff, so the wall simply drives them away

text: 1) Build a simple single-generator spreadsheet. 2) Vary parameters within reasonable ranges. 3) Plot generators owned over time, where each drop to zero marks a reset. 4) Check the spread of reset timing.
when: Balancing a prestige loop or modeling prestige behavior.
why: Sweeping parameters reveals how the loop behaves across likely player choices and captures most players, though individual reset behavior is hard to predict.

text: 1) Plot the progression curve over time. 2) Find the points where time-to-next-purchase spikes. 3) Treat each spike as a churn cliff and add a structural cure there.
when: Diagnosing where an idle game loses players
why: Spikes in waiting time mark the points where players are most likely to quit

text: Use structural fixes for stalls: a prestige reset, a fresh system that alters the optimization problem, limited-time events with temporary boosts, or social features giving outside reasons to return.
when: A progression wall or clicker fatigue needs fixing
why: These change the structure of play rather than simply slowing progress

text: Hidden formulas may drive the simulation, but visible consequences should drive player decisions.
Lifetime or max-based formulas reward continued progression, while since-reset formulas reward replaying the same point but yield diminishing returns beyond a point if the curve is flat.
when: Choosing a prestige currency measure.
why: The measure determines whether progress or repetition is rewarded.

text: Players learn to want prestige resets when the reset is framed as a fast-forward rather than a loss.
when: when presenting a prestige reset to players
why: Framing the reset as acceleration turns a sacrifice into a desired step.

text: A prestige reset asks the player to give up visible progress for permanent power, and the trade feels worthwhile when the next run is faster, opens new upgrade routes, or shifts bottlenecks.
when: when the player weighs whether to reset
why: the permanent gain must outweigh the visible progress lost

text: A voluntary prestige reset clears most current progress in exchange for prestige currency or a permanent multiplier; also called rebirth, ascension or reincarnation.
when: Designing a meta-progression loop; when a run's progression curve has flattened
why: Resetting trades visible progress for a faster next climb; turns repeated runs into faster, stronger cycles

text: Prestige resets grant a currency and a multiplier; their main jobs are the ladder-climbing feeling and keeping numbers in a manageable range.
Most prestige formulas use fractional exponents such as square or cube roots, not true logarithms, so currency can still grow very large.
Vary multiplier values per generator to produce shifting purchase priorities over time.
when: Designing generator progression.
why: Changing relative value keeps player choices from becoming fixed.

text: Vary reset timing like the rest of the run, with slow and fast stretches, arising from multipliers, upgrades, prestige-currency gain, and player reset choices.
when: Designing prestige loop pacing.
why: Uniform reset timing feels monotonous.

text: A dungeon run can award meta currency from floors cleared (since-reset) or deepest floor reached (max-based), and the choice determines whether replaying shallow floors stays rewarding.
when: Designing dungeon meta progression.
why: Measure choice sets reward for repetition versus progression.

text: A simple cost growth factor alone does not give relief; a dense layer of targeted multipliers is what lets production catch up with rising costs.
when: when a geometric cost curve starts outpacing income
why: Targeted boosts jump production at key moments, which closes the gap that cost growth opens.

text: Award one prestige token per fixed number of lifetime resources earned.
when: A simple prestige currency is needed
why: A flat rate is easy to explain and predict

text: Offer a prestige reset when progress meaningfully slows, so the reset feels like a fresh start with a real advantage.
when: Deciding when to offer a prestige reset
why: A reset is only attractive when the current run has stalled

text: Multipliers triggered at generator count thresholds cause bursts of rapid purchases as the player reaches each threshold.
when: Designing multipliers unlocked at generator milestones.
why: Players rush to reach the threshold.

text: Output comes from owned units plus stacked multipliers: milestone bonuses triggered when 25, 50, and 100 units are owned, one-time upgrades, and prestige multipliers.
when: when layering production boosts in an idle game
why: Stacked multipliers compound with unit count, letting output keep pace with geometric cost.

text: A meta-currency earned only by resetting is usually scaled to a measure of the run being given up, such as lifetime earnings.
when: when designing the currency a prestige reset grants
why: Scaling to the run given up rewards the sacrifice and makes each reset worth doing.

text: Meta-currency granted by resetting adds permanent production bonuses that persist across runs and speed up each later run.
when: when a prestige reset grants a persistent currency
why: Permanent bonuses make each new run climb faster than the last.

text: With a prestige exponent of 0.5, doubling currency requires four times the total XP, so short early resets are worth more than one long run.
when: Choosing the exponent of prestige currency
why: Diminishing returns reward multiple shorter cycles over a single long run

text: A stat's bonus multiplier starts at 1.0 and adds bonus-per-level times purchased level for each matching upgrade.
when: Several prestige upgrades affect the same stat
why: Additive stacking keeps each upgrade's contribution predictable

text: A square-root prestige curve gives large early bonus jumps and diminishing gains later, creating a difficulty curve without explicit level design.
when: when later resets should matter but be harder to justify
why: the square root slows growth as points rise

text: Prestige currency equals the floor of lifetime earnings raised to an exponent of 0.5 to 0.8, times a multiplier.
when: Calculating prestige currency from lifetime progress
why: Exponents below 1 give diminishing returns so repeated resets stay worthwhile

text: Layered prestige stacks resets where each layer clears everything beneath it and adds a new currency and optimization problem, such as an Ascension layer followed by an Eternity layer.
when: when a single reset loop would exhaust the optimization puzzle over very long play
why: Each new layer changes what the player solves, keeping a finite curve from feeling finished

text: Each prestige upgrade has four properties: the stat it affects, a bonus per level, a maximum level, and a first-level cost in prestige currency.
when: Designing permanent prestige upgrades
why: These fields define how fast and how far each upgrade scales

text: A preview below 1 token means no token is available, so the prestige prompt should not appear.
when: Checking whether a prestige reset would yield any currency
why: Showing a prompt with zero reward is confusing

text: Stacking prestige layers without changing the underlying problem each time only makes the numbers bigger, not the game fresher.
when: when adding prestige layers to an idle game
why: Larger numbers alone give no new decisions, so players stop caring about the extra layer.

text: 1) Divide current points by 1000. 2) Take the square root. 3) Round down to an integer bonus. 4) Set the permanent multiplier to 1 plus bonus times 0.1.
1) Run a periodic global tick about every 60 seconds. 2) Show the prestige prompt only if the preview gives at least 3 tokens and the current run has lasted at least 1800 seconds.
when: Deciding when to surface the prestige prompt
why: Thresholds prevent prompts that offer too little or appear too early

text: Make the next run noticeably faster within the first 30 seconds after a prestige reset; otherwise the reset reads as pure loss or punishment and players stop resetting.
when: when designing prestige rewards
why: Players need a visible faster recovery to justify giving up progress; otherwise the prestige system fails

text: A prestige reset clears resources and upgrades but keeps its permanent bonuses.
Anything representing player skill and knowledge persists through prestige, while anything representing in-game resources resets.
when: Deciding what a prestige reset keeps or clears
why: Keeping skill and knowledge preserves meaning, while resetting resources keeps the loop worthwhile

text: Add deeper prestige layers only when the earlier layer already feels rewarding and clear, and each layer stays understandable to the player.
Resetting early yields a small permanent reward, while waiting too long lets temporary progress stall; reset timing is itself a strategic choice.
Too much carry-over makes a prestige reset feel meaningless, while too little makes it feel punishing.
when: Choosing what a prestige reset keeps
why: Carry-over sets how much a reset feels like progress versus loss

text: Achievements serve three purposes: they give goals beyond the main path, reward desired behavior, and form a completion log showing percentage of content completed.
when: Designing achievements for a game
why: Achievements extend play beyond main progression and signal completion

text: Achievement categories include skill milestones, mastery milestones, collection, combat, crafting, economy, and completionist goals.
when: Organizing achievements by type
why: Covering several categories spreads goals across the game's systems

text: Use standard achievements for one-time events and incremental achievements for stats tracked against a target value.
when: Choosing an achievement type
why: One-time events unlock once while counts need progress tracking

text: Incremental games remove manual input over time, so automation is progression: repetition is replaced by broader allocation decisions.
when: Designing the progression of an incremental game.
why: Once the player understands an action, repeating it adds little.

text: Showing every upgrade and number at once removes the sense of mystery; reveal only the next few upgrades.
when: Presenting upgrade lists in an idle game
why: Full visibility removes discovery

text: In a derivative chain, each generator produces the tier below it, so tiers act as successive rates of change ending at the primary currency.
Generator cost typically grows exponentially while production grows linearly or polynomially, so costs eventually outpace output.
Exponential growth of the form n to the x eventually exceeds any polynomial growth, regardless of polynomial exponent or small base.
With n tiers the derivative chain's series approaches e^x as n grows, yet any finite chain stays sub-exponential, so exponential costs still outpace production.
when: Choosing the number of tiers in a derivative chain.
why: Finite tier counts bound the growth rate.

text: Tune dungeon reward or enemy difficulty growth with the same cost-versus-output formulas, so rewards do not outpace player power.
when: Designing dungeon run progression.
why: The same exponential-versus-polynomial seesaw governs both.

text: Small changes to the cost growth factor or production multipliers can turn a satisfying climb into a runaway or a dead-stop wall.
when: when adjusting idle-game cost and production ratios
why: Compounding makes the progression highly sensitive to small parameter changes.

text: Show a visible stock count for capped upgrades so the player knows how many purchases remain.
when: Shop items have a purchase cap
why: Without a visible limit, players cannot plan purchases

text: Growing upgrade costs by about 1.15× per level keeps upgrades reachable yet increasingly meaningful.
when: Choosing default idle upgrade cost growth
why: Exponential growth keeps each step feeling earned without becoming impossible

text: Use a derivative chain when you want the feeling of multiple stacked idle games, with lower tiers visibly growing large.
when: Aiming for layered, multi-stage growth.
why: Visible lower-tier growth creates the stacked-game sensation.

text: Keep lower tiers worth buying by tying them to purchased-count boosts or dependencies, so players keep spending resources in several ways.
when: Lower tiers would otherwise be produced for free and stop being worth buying.
why: Free production removes the reason to purchase.

text: Explore generator interactions beyond the two most common idle models; draw a flowchart of connections and experiment with the arrows.
when: Designing an idle game's generator structure.
why: Many interaction designs exist beyond the classic models.

text: When a build stalls in an idle game, let players re-specialize strategy rather than wait, which keeps optimization interest alive.
when: when a single-strategy idle game would flatten into pure waiting
why: Changing the strategy gives a new optimization problem instead of passive time-passing.

text: Upgrades should change what the player can do, not merely scale numbers; flat percentage gains are fine in moderation, yet standout upgrades alter the plan.
Basing generator cost on purchased count rather than total owned keeps manual purchases meaningful when automation supplies large free counts.
when: Generators also produced by higher tiers.
why: Free units would otherwise inflate cost and make purchases pointless.

text: Each tier in a derivative chain integrates the tier above it, so the currency series is 1, x, x²/2, x³/6, x⁴/24 and so on.
when: Stacking generator tiers where each feeds the one below.
why: Successive integration produces polynomial terms.

text: Per-unit cost growth factor for generators typically falls between 1.07 and 1.15; 1.07 raises each purchase cost by 7 percent, 1.15 by 15 percent.
when: Setting cost scaling for a chain of purchasable producers or idle-game generators.
why: Compounding production balances rising unit cost, and this band keeps costs rising without becoming unaffordable too fast.

text: An optimal income-to-cost model ranks generators by production gained per cost spent, predicting purchase priorities, though players tend to buy in bulk rather than follow it exactly.
when: Predicting which generator a player will buy next.
why: Players deviate from strictly optimal purchase order.

text: Applying bulk-buy or max-buy formulas to costs with shifting bases or changing exponents gives wrong results.
when: Costs change over time or the exponent is not fixed.
why: The closed forms assume constant base and growth rate.

text: If the newest generator always dominates on a log scale, older generators become irrelevant and purchase decisions lose meaning.
when: Tuning generator cost and output so each new tier overwhelms earlier ones.
why: Log-scale comparison hides the older tiers' contribution.

text: A cheap generator that looks better on paper may go unnoticed if its impact is too small for the player to feel.
when: Comparing generators by numeric value alone.
why: Players respond to perceived impact, not calculated value.

text: If output races ahead of costs, players purchase all at once and suspense dies; if costs race ahead of output, players hit a wall and stall.
when: when tuning the ratio of income to cost growth
why: Both extremes remove the tension between saving and buying, and the workable band between them is narrow.

text: Linear upgrade costs create long stretches where progress feels glacial and players stall.
when: Setting upgrade cost growth

text: Next generator cost equals base cost times growth rate raised to the number owned, so each purchase costs a fixed percentage more. Total production equals base production times owned times multipliers.
when: Pricing repeatable generators with exponential costs and a fixed growth rate.
why: Exponential growth makes late purchases costly and forces strategic choices.

text: 1) Multiply base price by growth rate raised to owned count. 2) Multiply by (growth rate to the power n, minus 1). 3) Divide by (growth rate minus 1). The result is total cost of buying n generators at once.
when: Costs follow simple exponential growth with fixed base and growth rate.
why: Closed form avoids looping over each purchase.

text: 1) Multiply currency by (growth rate minus 1). 2) Divide by base price times growth rate to the owned count. 3) Add 1. 4) Take log base growth rate. 5) Floor the result. This is the maximum number of generators affordable.
when: Costs follow simple exponential growth with fixed base and growth rate.
why: Closed form avoids looping over each purchase.

text: 1) Avoid one-step production. 2) Chain raw resources into intermediate materials. 3) Craft intermediates into equipment or food. For example, copper and tin ore make bronze bar, which makes bronze sword at Smithing 15.
when: Designing crafting systems
why: Multi-step chains give production depth and reason to gather several resources

text: 1) Ask whether the player can explain what changed without a calculator. 2) Ask whether the upgrade unlocks or improves a choice the player already understands. 3) Ask whether it stays relevant beyond the next thirty seconds.
when: when reviewing any upgrade before shipping

text: Aim for a roughly constant time until the next meaningful purchase, even as raw numbers grow; tune the production-to-cost ratio to control that interval.
when: when tuning progression pacing in an idle game
why: Players feel pace through the wait between meaningful decisions, not the magnitude of numbers.

text: Bulk purchase lets a player buy several room upgrades in one step, but only if those upgrade costs follow the same exponential pattern.
when: Applying bulk-buy to dungeon room upgrades or unlocks.
why: The closed-form formulas require the same exponential cost structure.

text: Designers may let lower tiers stay unbought; the boost becomes a choice rather than a requirement.
when: Deciding whether lower-tier purchases are mandatory.
why: Optional boosts preserve player agency.

text: Most skills run idle at full efficiency, while combat needs food management and can kill the player offline if set up wrongly, so combat rewards active attention.
when: Deciding which systems should run idle
why: Making only risky combat need attention keeps most play idle-friendly while rewarding focus where it matters

text: Identical numeric systems wrapped in different themes feel different to players because the narrative shapes how they respond.
when: Choosing a theme for a clicker or idle system
why: Players respond to narrative around the same numbers

text: Games are systems of meaningful decisions, so a shift from input to optimization matters because it moves the play toward choices.
The incremental genre centers on exponential, steadily building resource accumulation via repeated actions or automation.
when: Defining the incremental genre
why: Repetition and accumulation distinguish this genre from other games

text: Idle dungeon RPGs produce resources while the app is closed, show a summary on return, and run fully offline, combining buildings, production, storage, minions, upkeep, defense, research and upgrades.
Identify where the fun lies, such as unfolding features, collecting achievements, or optimizing the prestige loop, before optimizing numbers.
when: Early design, deciding which systems deserve most effort.
why: Systems that deliver the fun should be tuned first.

text: The real content of an incremental game is the decision layer, such as which upgrade path to take, which currency to prioritize, and when to reset.
when: Designing the mid and late game of an idle game.
why: Optimization decisions replace repetitive input as the source of engagement.

text: Treat early clicking as temporary onboarding and phase it out quickly, since the interesting game is optimization rather than tapping.
when: Designing early game input.
why: Repetitive tapping delays the decision layer.

text: A timed gathering action accumulates delta each tick; when the timer reaches zero or below, it completes, grants rewards, and resets to the mastery-adjusted duration.
when: Idle or skill actions running on a fixed cycle
why: Repeated timed cycles make each completion a predictable, countable reward event

text: Idle games have about 30 seconds to show they are interesting and about 4 minutes to show what happens next.
when: Designing idle game onboarding
why: Players decide quickly whether to keep attention on the game

text: Incremental games have three subtypes: clicker (active), idle (passive), and idle RPG (both active and passive).
when: Classifying an incremental game
why: Subtypes differ in how much active input the player gives

text: An idle RPG in this style needs several interlocking loops: skill, combat, mastery, and meta.
when: Designing the loop structure of an idle RPG
why: Interlocking loops feed each other so progress in one supports the others

text: The idle core loop is earn, spend, repeat: resources grow at rate times elapsed time, the rate is base rate times upgrade multiplier, and a prompt appears once resources reach the next cost.
Idle dungeon management keeps the player engaged through four recurring decisions: build, staff, balance, and sacrifice.
when: Designing idle dungeon management
why: Ongoing decisions keep automated play interesting

text: Relying on big numbers alone as the source of delight is no longer enough for players.
why: Novelty of large numbers has faded.

text: Minimizing waiting, the usual instinct in other genres, works against an idle game, where waiting is part of the product.
when: when designing pacing for a game built around absence
why: Waiting creates the anticipation that gives the return its value.

text: Depth on the scale of the largest established idle RPGs creates unmanageable scope for a solo developer.
when: Planning scope for a solo idle RPG
why: Many interlocking systems multiply content and testing work

text: Let the baseline run without the player and make active play an optional multiplier on top; presence should help but never be mandatory.
when: Designing idle game progression.
why: Mandatory activity turns the game into a chore.

text: Give every core loop instant feedback at each stage: action, resource gained, spend or invest, then grow stronger or faster.
when: Designing a core loop
why: Immediate feedback at each stage keeps the loop satisfying

text: Active play gives immediate advantages such as higher-tier actions and better combat setups, while idle play runs only the last selected action; balance them so neither makes the other pointless.
when: Designing rewards for active and offline play
why: If idle matches active play, active play loses value; if idle is too weak, idle play feels pointless

text: Idle games balance exponentially rising generator costs against slower production growth; prestige resets and multipliers reset that balance.
Common idle-game monetization forms are time skips that collect hours of production, timed production boosters, permanent multipliers bought with premium currency, and rewarded video ads.
when: when planning monetization for an idle game
why: Each form accelerates progress the player is already making, so it fits the core loop.

text: Offline progression can simulate up to 24 hours, with mastery XP earned offline and farming not auto-replanting.
when: Designing offline progression limits
why: A cap bounds catch-up time and clarifies which activities run offline

text: Keep offline simulation of dungeon runs careful, since under-prepared offline combat is dangerous.
when: Simulating dungeon runs while the player is away
why: Offline fights without player input can end in death if setup is weak

text: Show a welcome-back summary of offline gains only when the gap is meaningful, skipping very short gaps.
when: Player returns after being away
why: Summaries for trivial gaps add noise without informing the player

text: Offline caps and booster timers create scarcity, and a rewarded ad that relieves that scarcity at the return moment reaches non-paying players too.
when: when designing offline earnings and rewarded ads together
why: The return moment is when the player feels the windfall, so an offer there is both timely and broadly reachable.

text: Crafting uses a queue, and offline crafting processes queued items until materials run out.
when: Designing offline production in an idle game
why: A queue lets production continue while the player is away until inputs are exhausted

text: A common offline compromise pays full or near-full output for a cap of roughly a handful of hours up to about a day, occasionally at a slightly lower rate.
when: when choosing an offline cap for an idle game
why: A bounded window keeps return rewards generous without unlimited unattended progress.

text: Offline earnings equal base rate times hours away times 0.5, rewarding absence at half the active rate.
when: Computing offline earnings for an idle game

text: Idle RPGs have three play modes: active (manual choices and food management in combat), idle (leaving the game running or closing it), and offline (a welcome-back summary).
when: Designing how players engage with an idle RPG
why: Each mode offers a different level of player attention

text: A model that treats income as per-second ignores timers, so slower high-tier generators are over-favored.
when: Building a generator priority model that ignores production timers.
why: Timer-based generators produce in discrete cycles, not continuously.

text: When basic progress for non-paying players is sluggish enough to feel like a paywall, a beloved game becomes a resented one.
when: when setting free-player pacing alongside paid acceleration
why: Players who feel forced to pay for basic progress resent the game and may leave.

text: Requiring active play to make any progress causes burnout.
when: Designing progress rates for active and idle play
why: Forced attention wears players out

text: Offline simulation counts every action as fully completed and ignores interrupted or partial cycles, so it can overstate offline output.
when: Offline progress uses whole-action division
why: Division by action time assumes no partial cycle at the boundary

text: If the reduced offline reward is too small, absence feels wasted and players stop returning.
when: Tuning offline reward rate

text: A shop item restock-time field can exist in data while the service ignores it, so restock behavior must be implemented explicitly.
when: Shop data includes a restock time but the service does not read it
why: A field with no logic gives players false expectations about availability

text: 1) Record active skill and action on leave, and timestamp on every save. 2) On load, compute elapsed time capped at 86,400 seconds (24 hours). 3) Divide by action time, rounded down, to count completed actions. 4) Roll loot and XP once per action, awarding mastery too. 5) Apply gains and show total on return.
when: when implementing offline progress for an idle game
why: Recording the activity lets the game replay it on return; a capped payout rewards returning without replacing active play.

text: Make active play more efficient than idle play while keeping idle play meaningful.
when: Balancing active and idle progress
why: If idle progress equals active progress, active play has no purpose; rewarding attention keeps both modes useful.

text: Design the return reward to unlock something and open a player choice, not just display a larger number.
when: when designing offline return rewards
why: A bare total gives no reason to act.

text: Use acceleration-based monetization only when the free loop is already satisfying, so paying players simply want the same progress faster.
when: when deciding how monetization relates to the free game
why: Selling speed on a fun loop feels fair; selling relief from a dull loop does not rescue it.

text: Design the welcome-back payout as a deliberate set piece that pays out accumulated progress in one hit on return.
when: when a player returns to an idle game after time away
why: A single ceremonial payout turns returning into a rewarding moment rather than a status check.

text: Use an offline-first structure when the game's depth lies in choosing what to pursue rather than in moment-to-moment execution.
when: when deciding whether a game should progress mainly while the player is away
why: Strategic choices can be made in short active sessions while the timer handles execution.

text: Uncapped clock-based offline progress gives accurate full returns after long absences but removes reason to return often; a cap rewards regular check-ins.
when: when deciding whether offline gains are capped
why: Elapsed clock time gives an accurate production basis, but capping trades that accuracy for more frequent returns.

text: Too little offline payout punishes players who cannot check in often, while too much makes active play pointless.
when: when setting how much progress accrues while the game is closed
why: Offline generosity must balance rewarding absent players against keeping active play worthwhile.

text: Space unlocks so a new item tier or ability arrives roughly every hour, e.g. every 10 skill levels; gaps of several hours with nothing new make players quit.
when: Placing unlocks along the progression curve or designing level-based unlock intervals
why: Regular unlocks keep players within reach of something new; long gaps make players quit.

text: Time phase transitions to roughly 3 to 5 minutes of active play; rushed or front-loaded content burns players out, sluggish content drives them away; leave room for later phases.
when: Pacing phase transitions in idle games, or moving early milestones earlier

text: Place milestones frequently early on, such as a level-up every few minutes, rather than only once a day.
when: Early game of an incremental game
why: Frequent rewards sustain engagement while players are still learning the systems

text: Even a simple visible milestone, such as a large resource target, gives players a direction to play toward.
when: Adding goals to an idle game

text: The strongest upgrades change how the player plays, such as moving from manual clicking to passive income, rather than only enlarging a number.
when: Designing upgrades for the early and mid game
why: Changing the player's role keeps upgrades meaningful

text: Faction-style alignments that change building bonuses and playstyle make strategic choices genuine, not cosmetic reskins.
when: when offering alignment choices in an idle game
why: Alignments that alter the whole strategy give players a meaningful decision with real consequences.

text: A progression wall is a stretch where cost growth outpaces income, leaving the player stalled for hours with nothing meaningful to do.
when: Cost growth outpaces income in an idle or incremental game
why: Income cannot keep pace with rising costs, so purchases stop and players stall

text: Early targets: first upgrade purchasable within 60 seconds, first automation within 3 minutes, first prestige within 10-15 minutes.
when: Pacing an idle game's opening

text: Idle RPG progression can run on two tracks: skill levels that unlock content, and per-item mastery that rewards repeated use of a specific item.
when: Designing depth in an idle RPG
why: Two tracks reward both breadth across skills and depth within each item

text: Progression by hours played has four stages: early (0-2h) with fast unlocks and constant discovery; mid (2-20h) with interacting systems and clear goals; late (20-100h) with slow mastery and optimization; end (100h+) with final goals, prestige or expansions.
when: Planning the pacing of a long game
why: Each stage needs a different kind of reward density and goal type

text: Idle games with no prestige or endgame goal lose players after the first session.
when: Designing long-term structure of an idle game
why: Players lack a direction to keep playing

text: 1) Player supplies input by clicking. 2) First generator produces without the player. 3) Later automation removes collection too. 4) Mid-game the game shifts from input to optimization.
when: Structuring an incremental game's early to mid progression.
why: Each step removes manual work in favor of decisions.

text: An exponential XP curve feels slow early and steep at high levels, so late levels take far more XP than early ones.
when: Designing long progression with many levels
why: Cost grows exponentially with level

text: Skill content is defined as data resources: a skill holds identifier, name, description, icon, type, action list and mastery checkpoints; an action holds required level, required items, base time, XP, mastery XP and loot table; a loot entry holds item, min and max quantity and chance.
In an idle game, art and theme cannot rescue a failing progression curve, because the numbers do most of the emotional work.
when: when evaluating an idle game's emotional impact
why: Players feel progress through the numbers, so a broken curve cannot be hidden by presentation.

text: Start with 5 to 8 skills rather than the full set for a first game, and start with one combat style before adding all three.
when: Scoping a first idle RPG
why: Full depth creates unmanageable scope for a solo developer

text: Hiring a manager for a generator makes it run permanently without input, so play shifts from collecting payouts to optimizing upgrades, multipliers and timing.
when: when a clicker-style income source is automated by a hired unit
why: Automation removes the repetitive action and leaves decisions about investment and timing as the remaining play.

text: Per-item mastery from 0 to 99 can reduce action time, increase yield, or reduce crafting cost for that item.
when: Designing per-item mastery benefits
why: Item-specific bonuses reward repeated use of the same item

text: In the example, Hitpoints XP is 1.3 percent of damage dealt, and Attack and Strength XP are each 30 percent of damage dealt.
when: Tuning combat XP rewards
why: Tying XP to damage rewards dealing damage in combat

text: Action time shrinks linearly with mastery, from 0% reduction at mastery 1 to 15% reduction at mastery 99.
when: Computing mastery-adjusted action duration

text: Per-item mastery uses a gentler polynomial table of 100 × level^1.2 for levels up to 99.
when: Setting per-item mastery progression
why: A polynomial grows more slowly than the main exponential curve

text: A large idle RPG can run 29 skills, 9 combat and 20 non-combat, each reaching level 120, with an extra tier extending 60 levels beyond that.
when: Scoping a large idle RPG skill set
why: Large skill counts show the depth a mature idle RPG can reach

text: XP for level n equals a base times n raised to an exponent; exponent 1.2 suits mastery systems, 1.5 suits idle RPGs with many skills, and 2.0 gives steeper quadratic growth.
when: Designing an XP curve for levels
why: The exponent controls how steep the late-game wall feels

text: A shared per-skill mastery pool takes 25% of mastery XP, spendable on any item; skill XP multiplies by 1.01, 1.03, 1.05, 1.10 at 10, 25, 50, 95% pool.
when: Designing mastery progression across items in a skill
why: A shared pool connects item mastery to skill-wide rewards

text: The main XP table accumulates per level floor(n + 300 × 2^(n/7)), divides the running total by 4 and floors it, producing a steep curve; level 1 is set to 0 XP.
when: Building an exponential level progression

text: Check the XP exponent against target completion times, because small changes strongly alter how steep the late game feels.
when: Tuning an XP curve
why: Exponent choice compounds into large differences in total time

text: 1) For each loot entry, roll against its chance. 2) If it succeeds, pick a quantity within its min-max range. 3) Add the items to inventory.
when: When a timed action completes

text: Require matching skill levels for each equipment tier, roughly level 1 for bronze and 15 to 20 for iron in both Mining and Smithing.
when: Gating equipment tiers behind skills
why: Matching gates tie each tier to skill progress in the relevant skills

text: Gate progression by skill level rather than by time alone, so players control their own path.
when: Designing unlocks for skill-based content
why: Agency over the path keeps players invested in choices

text: Only start a skill action when the player's skill level meets the action's required level.
when: Starting any skill action

text: A dungeon is a fixed challenge above normal area farming: the player must defeat a set enemy sequence ending in a boss, without swapping gear or food mid-run, for rewards unavailable elsewhere.
when: Designing structured challenges beyond open-ended farming
why: Fixed sequences and guaranteed rare rewards differentiate dungeons from farming

text: Combat level is the average of attack, strength, defence and hitpoints levels, rounded down.
when: Computing a player's combat level for requirement checks
why: A single averaged number gives one comparable measure of combat readiness

text: Combat is the spine of progression, and other skills feed into combat power.
when: Designing how skills connect to progression
why: Linking all skills to combat gives every skill a purpose

text: Combat uses three styles (melee, ranged, magic) with auto-combat, and auto-eat triggers when HP drops below a threshold.
when: Designing combat automation and styles
why: Automation lets idle combat run safely while still offering choice of style

text: Some games make automation the theme as well as the mechanic: the fiction shows the player handing control over production to systems, mirroring what the mechanics do.
when: when designing a game whose core loop shifts from player action to system-run production
why: Fiction and mechanics that express the same handoff of agency reinforce each other.

text: A boss special attack can kill the player, which must then trigger the normal death handler.
when: Implementing a boss special attack
why: Scripted damage is still real damage and must follow the death path

text: Max HP is 10 per Hitpoints level in the example, so level 1 has 10 HP and level 99 has 990 HP.
when: Scaling player health with level
why: Linear scaling keeps HP growth predictable

text: Critical hits deal 50 percent bonus damage.
when: Designing critical hit effects
why: A fixed bonus gives crits a clear, noticeable payoff

text: A dungeon run or expedition can act as one loop inside a larger meta loop, feeding rewards into the next run.
when: Structuring a dungeon inside a larger progression loop
why: Nested loops let each run contribute to long-term progress

text: When combat resolves on its own, the player's role shifts from executing fights to choosing what to train and which gear to equip.
when: when an idle RPG automates combat
why: Removing manual execution moves meaningful decisions to planning and preparation.

text: A boss phase threshold changes behavior once HP drops below a set value, here gaining damage reduction at 50% HP, giving a boss feel without a separate combat mode.
when: Adding a boss feel within the existing combat loop
why: A threshold switches the boss's stats or behavior inside the same tick-based combat

text: A boss special attack fires a guaranteed hit of 15% of its max HP, reduced by player damage reduction, when HP first crosses the threshold, and fires only once.
when: Adding a scripted burst at a boss phase change
why: A one-time guaranteed hit at the threshold creates a dramatic moment without repeating

text: Combat runs on a fixed tick, where each combatant's attack bar fills by speed times tick and attacks when full.
when: Building idle combat with attack timing
why: Fixed ticks make attack timing deterministic and simple to simulate

text: Accuracy and max hit use an effective-level formula, and hit chance depends on attacker accuracy compared to defender defence.
when: Computing hit chance and max hit in combat
why: Comparing attacker accuracy to defender defence determines how often attacks land

text: Dungeon-building idle games usually juggle interlocking systems: construction, output, capacity, worker dispatch, maintenance costs, guarding, and permanent upgrades plus lab work.
Food and combat setup matter when offline, and underprepared combat can kill the player.
when: Designing offline combat
why: Offline fights run without player input, so preparation must be sufficient

text: 1) Start with easy enemies. 2) Repeat them once. 3) Introduce a new enemy type or mechanic. 4) Combine known threats into a first real challenge. 5) End with a boss.
when: Ordering enemies in a fixed dungeon sequence
why: Escalating in steps lets players learn each new threat before facing combinations

text: Require the player to plan their loadout before entering a dungeon, because gear and food cannot be swapped mid-run.
when: Designing a dungeon run
why: Fixed runs make preparation the main decision before the fight

text: Show dungeon difficulty through a required combat level on the dungeon.
when: Presenting dungeon difficulty to the player
why: A visible level requirement communicates difficulty before entry

text: Fight dungeon waves as sequential single enemies, with no pause between them.
when: Structuring a dungeon enemy sequence
why: Sequential one-at-a-time fights keep the pacing continuous

text: Tie each dungeon to a new content tier so every clear unlocks something new, such as an area, enemy set, crafting material, or endgame content.
when: Designing the sequence of dungeons across a game
why: Each unlock gives a reason to clear the next dungeon

text: Make Cooking a gate for harder combat, since cooked food is consumed directly in combat.
when: Linking production skills to combat readiness
why: Consumed food makes cooking directly relevant to survival in fights

text: Dungeons offer structured, planned challenge with guaranteed rare rewards, while open area farming offers open-ended play where the player can stop at any time.
when: Choosing between structured challenges and open-ended play
why: Fixed runs demand planning and commitment, while farming allows flexible stopping

text: Dungeon enemy sequences can end with a boss, with food and equipment fixed for the run unless upgraded.
when: Structuring generated dungeon runs
why: A boss ending with fixed loadout gives a clear endpoint to each run

text: Storage, upkeep and defense constraints are layout pressures that a dungeon generator's output must satisfy.
when: when generating dungeon layouts for dungeon-building idle games

text: A dungeon data definition holds: ID, name, description, icon, required combat level, recommended food, ordered enemy IDs, boss ID, reward entries, and estimated duration in minutes.
when: Authoring static dungeon data
why: These fields together describe everything the game needs to run and display a dungeon

text: Mastery bonus tiers described as ranges must be resolved by the integer-level checks in code, since boundary values decide which bonus applies.
when: Implementing tiered mastery bonuses
why: Range wording is ambiguous at exact thresholds

text: 1) Record the clear and increment the clear count. 2) Roll each reward entry against its chance. 3) Add each rolled quantity to the player. 4) Emit a clear event.
when: A player completes a dungeon
why: Ordered handling ensures rewards and progress are recorded consistently

text: Store clear status and clear counts in save data, not in the static dungeon definition.
when: Persisting dungeon progress
why: Keeping per-save state out of the definition keeps the definition reusable across saves

text: Refuse dungeon entry when the player's combat level is too low or when they hold fewer than 5 food items.
when: Validating dungeon entry
why: Entry checks prevent starting a run the player cannot survive

text: Advance game systems each frame using accumulated delta time rather than a timer node, which makes offline simulation simpler to run.
when: Designing a game loop that must also support offline progress
why: A shared tick path lets the same logic run live and offline

text: A fixed pacing template (easy, repeat, new mechanic, combined, then boss) can order procedurally generated encounters per room layout, teaching each mechanic before combining them.
when: Generating dungeon encounters procedurally
why: A fixed sequence with a boss ending gives a predictable structure to fill with generated content; the pattern teaches each mechanic before combining them, then ends on a boss

text: A chain of spawn or production tiers, where each tier feeds the one below, can model layered resource flow in a dungeon economy.
when: Designing dungeon resource systems.
why: Layered feeding mirrors stacked production.

text: Tying each stage to a specific unlocked area lets generated floors gate deeper zones.
when: Generating layered dungeon content
why: Gating deeper zones behind earlier clears gives generated content a progression structure

text: Apply the faucet-and-sink check to any reward a generator produces, such as loot or currency per room, to confirm it has a sink.
when: Generating rewards procedurally
why: Generated rewards without a sink accumulate uselessly, just like hand-placed currency

text: In generated dungeons, dungeon clears can be standard achievements and enemies defeated can be incremental achievements.
when: Adding achievements to procedurally generated content
why: Mapping existing events to achievement types reuses the same tracking

text: After a big milestone, players who just reached it tend to keep playing in a fast section, so simulated reset timing becomes inaccurate.
when: Just after a major milestone is reached.
why: Momentum keeps players in the run.

text: Random-timed optional bonuses that grant large temporary boosts encourage players to keep part of their attention on the game while idle players lose only the bonus.
when: Designing optional active boosts with random spawn timing.
why: Unpredictable timing creates a hook for attention.

text: Players of idle games value anticipation and the return moment, since most of the game's activity happens while they are away.
when: when the player is not expected to stay present
why: Looking forward to a reward is itself a source of pleasure, so the return is the high point.

text: Clicker fatigue appears when input becomes tedious mashing, or when nothing remains but waiting, and players then tend to quit.
when: Active input turns into repetitive mashing or only waiting remains
why: Repetitive input and empty waiting drain player motivation

text: Seasonal events and double-output windows cost little to host and hand inactive players a dated reason to reopen the game.
when: Players have lapsed and need a reason to return
why: A dated window creates urgency and a concrete reason to come back

text: Penalizing time away through rotting stockpiles, lost streaks, or progress that accrues only while foregrounded breeds anxiety and eventually churn.
when: Designing offline and return mechanics.
why: Players feel pressured and eventually quit.

text: Artisan crafts consume ingredients at craft start and output at timer end; a queued quantity repeats while ingredients remain, so a mid-craft stop leaves input cost paid.
when: Designing crafting with inputs and queued repeats
why: Upfront consumption means interruptions waste inputs

text: Balancing progression is hard; spreadsheet models help, but iteration is required, and many tools are available.

1) Model cost and income curves in a spreadsheet. 2) At each progression stage, compute time until the next meaningful purchase. 3) Check whether that interval stays roughly constant. 4) Flag stages where it spikes, since players are likely to quit there.
when: when tuning an idle game's progression before a balance pass
why: Measuring the interval targets what players actually feel rather than raw magnitude.

text: 1) Play as a new player. 2) Check whether a meaningful decision point is reached within 5 minutes. 3) Revise the opening if not.
when: Auditing an early-game onboarding sequence
why: New players decide quickly whether to keep playing

text: 1) Listen to game events such as level-up, enemy defeat, dungeon clear, craft completed, and mastery level-up. 2) Update the relevant stat from every such event, since missed event coverage leaves progress unrecorded.
when: Implementing or checking achievement progress tracking against game events
why: Tracking from every relevant event prevents missed progress; gaps in event coverage leave some progress unrecorded

text: A strict byte budget forces every feature to earn its place, producing tighter and more focused games.
Small browser idle games can ship at 4 to 30 KB with no framework, a size at which they load before the player's attention wanders.
Vanilla JavaScript with no framework, engine or dependencies keeps idle browser games very small, which matters because load time strongly affects whether players stay.
when: when building browser games where load time decides retention
why: a multi-hundred-kilobyte game shows a loading bar and loses attention

text: Record dungeon clears in a separate progress table so the static dungeon definition stays reusable across saves.
when: Storing dungeon clear progress
why: Separating progress from definitions keeps definitions reusable

text: Treating generator output as continuous can cause confusion when a generator is created within the same tick; handle the partial production explicitly.
when: Implementing generators that produce in discrete time steps.
why: Continuous assumptions break on newly created units.

text: Define skills, actions and loot as data resources so new actions can be added without changing skill code.
when: Building content for a skill system
why: Keeps content changes out of code paths

text: Level-from-XP lookups that search downward from the top level must handle the highest level boundary explicitly.
when: Converting total XP to level

text: If the language lacks a log function for an arbitrary base, divide the natural or common log of the inner expression by the natural or common log of the growth rate.
when: Computing max affordable count in a language without arbitrary-base logarithms.
why: Change-of-base identity gives the same result.

text: 1) Build the XP table once on first use. 2) Every lookup calls the build step first. 3) Read values from the cached array.
when: Serving level-XP lookups from a precomputed table
why: Avoids recalculating the curve on each lookup

text: Track total owned and purchased counts separately so the system can distinguish player-built features from automation-produced ones.
when: Designing dungeon systems with automated and built features.
why: Mixing the two counts hides which features the player chose.

text: Each shop item defines an ID, the granted item, a display name, a gold cost, a quantity per purchase, a purchase cap where 0 means unlimited, a restock time where 0 means always available, and an optional skill level requirement.
when: Building a data-driven shop
why: A complete item record lets one service handle every shop entry

text: 1) Confirm the item exists. 2) Confirm gold covers the total cost. 3) Confirm the purchase cap is not exceeded. 4) Confirm any level requirement is met. 5) On success remove gold, grant the item, record the purchase count and emit a purchase-completed event.
when: Processing a shop purchase
why: Checks before granting prevent invalid or unaffordable transactions

text: 1) When a purchase cap applies, reduce the requested quantity to the remaining allowed purchases. 2) Complete the purchase with the reduced quantity.
when: A bulk purchase exceeds the remaining cap
why: Trimming the quantity avoids rejecting a partly valid order

text: Refresh the shop panel when items are added or removed and when a purchase completes.
when: Shop inventory or purchase state changes
why: Stale rows would show wrong costs or stock

text: Trigger a boss special attack only when HP crosses the threshold from above, using a flag so it fires once.
when: Implementing a one-time boss event at an HP threshold
why: Checking the crossing direction and a flag prevents repeated firing

text: 1) Multiply the XP amount by the XP multiplier inside the skill's XP-adding method. 2) Store the result as the new XP value.
when: Applying a prestige or upgrade XP multiplier
why: Applying it at one central point ensures every XP gain is boosted

text: The estimated dungeon duration shown to players is a UI hint calculated from the total enemy HP in the run.
when: Displaying expected dungeon length
why: Enemy HP totals approximate how long the fight will take

text: Completion percent equals unlocked achievement count divided by total definitions, times 100.
when: Showing completion progress in a log
why: A simple ratio gives players a clear measure of overall completion

text: 1) Multiply the per-second value by 3,600. 2) Append '/hr' and an optional unit.
when: Showing production rates to players
why: Session-length rates are easier to judge than per-second values

text: Animate resource or XP gains with a brief floating label, such as '+42 XP', and a gold tint on skill panels, without modal interruption instead of silent value updates.
when: A player gains a resource or XP, including level-ups
why: Transient visual gain feedback makes progress feel rewarding and confirms it while play continues

text: Show per-time rates alongside totals, such as 'logs per hour' or 'XP per hour'.
when: Progress accumulates over time in an idle or incremental game
why: Rates let players judge how fast they are growing

text: Show completion logs that indicate how close the player is to 100 percent.
when: Collection or completion goals exist
why: A visible completion measure gives players a clear next target

text: Show time as hours, minutes and seconds, dropping leading units that are zero.
when: Displaying durations to players

text: Show a skill's progress bar as XP earned within the current level against XP required for the next level.
when: Displaying skill progress

text: When progress slows, the game should explain the cause and present a minimum of two sensible remedies.
Exponential notation compresses runaway growth so each tenfold increase reads as a small step in the exponent, making relentless growth feel steady.
when: when displaying numbers that grow by orders of magnitude
why: Small exponent increments represent huge value jumps, so the growth feels smooth rather than overwhelming.

text: Standard floating-point numbers top out around 1.8e308, so very large idle-game values overflow and need a custom big-number representation.
when: when idle-game values grow beyond standard float range
why: Native float types cannot represent magnitudes past their maximum.

text: Fixed formatting thresholds make values just below and above a boundary look different, which can confuse players reading the number.
when: Choosing number formatting thresholds
why: Format switches at discrete points

text: Pick a default number notation that fits the game's tone, and provide a toggle, since identical values may read as warm or sterile depending on formatting.
when: when designing number display for an idle or incremental game
why: Players differ in the feel they prefer, and notation shapes how growth is perceived.

text: When the reward is just a counter climbing higher, number typography forms a central part of game feel and deserves design care.
when: when the main reward in a game is a growing counter
why: The displayed number carries the reward, so its form directly shapes how satisfying progress feels.

text: Plain integers under 1,000 with K/M/B suffixes at one or two decimals, or comma grouping to 10,000 then one-decimal K to 1 million and two-decimal M, B, T beyond.
when: when displaying totals that grow into thousands, millions or billions
why: Raw long integers are hard to read and make growth hard to perceive; suffixes keep big numbers readable.

text: Suffix notation (thousand, million, letter suffixes) feels warm and human early on, while scientific notation is colder but unlimited and precise at large scales.
when: when choosing how large idle-game numbers are displayed
why: Familiar words suit early numbers; scientific form keeps working when suffixes run out.

text: A base resolution of 1920 by 1080 with canvas-items stretch and expand aspect scales the UI to varying screen sizes.
when: Setting up a fixed-base-resolution UI

text: Greedy ad placement works as a tax on the fun, so ads placed to maximize views damage the play they are meant to monetize.
when: when placing rewarded or interstitial ads in a game
why: Interruptions at the wrong moment erode the enjoyment that makes players return.

text: Containers arrange children automatically, so manually positioning those children conflicts with the container layout.
when: Placing controls inside containers

text: Long skill or recipe lists overflow unless wrapped in a scroll container.
when: Displaying lists longer than the screen

text: 1) Create a base style box. 2) Duplicate it for each state: normal, hover, pressed, disabled. 3) Change only the color on each copy.
when: Styling interactive buttons across states

text: 1) Add incoming notifications to a queue. 2) Show one notification at a time. 3) Keep each visible for its duration, default 2.5 seconds, before showing the next.
when: Displaying multiple timed notifications
why: Sequential display avoids stacked popups

text: 1) State how long the game advanced. 2) State what was earned. 3) Say if a limit or efficiency factor altered the outcome.
when: Showing offline progress on return
why: Players need the basis of the number to trust it

text: The return screen should show elapsed time, animate the earned amount, and point immediately to what the windfall can now buy.
when: when designing the welcome-back screen for an idle game
why: A receipt wastes the anticipation built during absence, while an animated payout with a clear next step drives re-engagement.

text: Sort dungeons by required level, show clear counts when any exist, and disable the enter button with the refusal reason as a tooltip.
when: Designing the dungeon selection panel
why: Level ordering shows progression and tooltips explain why entry is blocked

text: Show locked achievements grayed out and hidden achievements as question marks until unlocked in the completion log.
when: Displaying an achievement grid
why: Grayed and hidden states show what remains without spoiling hidden goals

text: Apply one shared theme resource to the root control so child controls inherit consistent styling.
when: Building a multi-screen idle game UI
why: Inheritance keeps styling uniform across screens

text: Keep tooltips on a top layer that follows the mouse with a small offset and clamps inside the screen edges.
when: Showing hover tooltips
why: Clamping prevents tooltips from leaving the visible area

text: Gated content: show grayed out with requirement as goal; in shops, hide unmet-level items but show each cost, quantity selector, and remaining stock for capped items.
when: when content is gated behind a requirement, or when rendering a shop panel
why: A visible requirement turns locked content into a target, while hiding locked shop items avoids clutter and stock and quantity controls support informed buying.
